name: Lutein and zeaxanthin supplements

card.summary: Plant carotenoids sold for eye health; the research is about macular degeneration, not cosmetic eye brightness, and its overall result there is modest.
card.aka: Lutein, zeaxanthin, macular pigment supplements, marigold extract
card.note: Studied for age-related macular degeneration, not for cosmetic eye appearance; excess intake can cause harmless skin yellowing (carotenodermia).

quick.overview:
Lutein and zeaxanthin are yellow plant pigments (xanthophyll carotenoids) found in leafy greens and egg yolks. They concentrate in the macula, the central part of the retina, and are sold as over-the-counter supplements marketed for eye health.

Most research concerns age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and cataract rather than how the eyes look. A large US trial (AREDS2) and a later Cochrane review are the main reference points; they report small or no overall effects on AMD progression.
quick.mechanism: The pigments accumulate in the macula, where they are thought to filter blue light and act as antioxidants, although their exact functional role there is described as not fully established. Supplement studies often measure macular pigment density or visual function.
quick.risks: Excess intake of carotenoids is associated with a harmless yellow-orange skin tint (carotenodermia). Lutein is sold as a dietary supplement in the US and approved as a food additive (E161b) in the EU. Supplements are not a studied treatment for eye whiteness or brightness.

lead: Lutein and zeaxanthin are xanthophyll carotenoids, yellow pigments made by plants and obtained by people from foods such as leafy greens and egg yolks. They are isomers that the body can interconvert, and they accumulate in the macula of the retina [1][2]. Supplements combining the two are marketed mainly for eye health and are a large segment of the dietary-supplement market [1].

In appearance-focused communities, eye-health supplements are sometimes discussed alongside claims of clearer or brighter-looking eyes. The published research, however, addresses medical outcomes such as age-related macular degeneration (AMD), cataract, macular pigment density and visual function, not cosmetic appearance [2][3].

The largest trial, the Age-Related Eye Disease Study 2 (AREDS2), enrolled 4,203 participants [3]. As summarised in encyclopedic sources, adding lutein and zeaxanthin showed no overall benefit on AMD progression, though a subgroup with low dietary intake showed a reduction of roughly a quarter, and a 2023 Cochrane review concluded the supplements have little effect compared with placebo on AMD progression [1].
infobox: Leafy greens, egg yolk, marigold petal extract

paras: Lutein is made only by plants; animals obtain it through diet. It is abundant in kale and spinach and present in egg yolks. Zeaxanthin is its isomer and the two can be interconverted in the body [1]. Commercial supplements are commonly extracted from Mexican marigold petals [1].
Both pigments are found concentrated in the human macula, though encyclopedic sources note that their precise functional role there is not fully established [1].

AREDS2 was a phase 3 trial in people with or at risk of age-related macular degeneration and cataract, enrolling 4,203 participants from 2006 [3]. Summaries report that the lutein and zeaxanthin formulation did not reduce AMD progression overall, with a possible reduction in people whose diets were low in these carotenoids, and no overall reduction in cataract surgery [1]. A 2023 Cochrane review is described as finding little effect on AMD progression versus placebo and insufficient evidence for early AMD [1].

Smaller registered trials have examined other outcomes, including visual function in healthy people (terminated, n=14) [4], vision in people with albinism (n=10) [5], supplementation in pregnancy (phase 2, n=47) [6], macular pigment density in people with and without wet AMD (n=200) [7], night vision (n=27) [8], dry eye (n=110) [9] and retinal ageing (n=88) [10]. A planned trial in menopausal women is registered to examine cognition [11]. The registry entries describe designs and populations rather than results, and no registered trial listed here targets cosmetic eye appearance.

The only well-established effect of excessive intake is carotenodermia, a yellow-orange skin tint. Encyclopedic sources give an observed safe level of 20 mg/day and note that US and European authorities have not set an upper intake limit [1]. Lutein is approved as a food additive (E161b) in the EU and Australia and New Zealand; in the US it is permitted in supplements but not as a colouring for human foods [1].

timeline.event: AREDS2, a phase 3 trial of lutein and zeaxanthin among other nutrients, begins enrolment [3].
AREDS2 results are published; lutein and zeaxanthin show no overall benefit on AMD progression in the main analysis [1].
A Cochrane review reports little effect of the supplements on AMD progression compared with placebo [1].
